     change the CLI and regenerate, or the file will lie to whoever reads it. -->

# The `oculus` CLI

`--json` is the one global flag: it works on every command below,
and is listed once here rather than repeated in each section.

```
Sync Canvas subjects and lectures into your local Oculus library

Usage: oculus [OPTIONS] [COMMAND]

Commands:
  status      Session, library and parse status
  auth        Sign in to Canvas, or sign out
  keyd        Install, inspect or remove oculus-keyd, the credential broker
  list        List subjects or lectures
  run         Scrape Canvas content or sync lectures
  index       Re-parse and re-embed PDFs already on record
  search      Search the library by meaning (needs network and an API key)
  grep        Search the library by pattern (offline, no model)
  read        Print the text of one library file
  files       List the files in the library
  calendar    Class times and assignment due dates
  project     Plan work: projects, their boards, and what is on them
  task        Add, move, refile, finish and delete tasks, on a board or on none
  tag         List, add, rename, recolour and delete the tags tasks carry
  memory      Read and write the memory store the agents keep in the library
  lecture     Look inside a downloaded lecture recording
  transcribe  Transcribe a video that has no captions, on Groq or on this Mac
  studio      Make, render, check and narrate Studio videos: TSX scenes drawn frame by
              frame
  docs        Write the agent-facing docs into the library
  agent       Run one prompt through a CLI agent (Claude Code, Codex, opencode or
              Antigravity)
  help        Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s)

Options:
      --json
          Print machine-readable JSON instead of formatted text

          Honoured by every command that prints: status, list, search, grep, read,
          files, calendar, project, task, tag, keyd and studio. On failure the JSON is
          `{"error": "..."}` on stderr and the exit code is 1.

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

  -V, --version
          Print version
```

## `oculus auth`

```
Sign in to Canvas, or sign out

Usage: oculus auth <COMMAND>

Commands:
  canvas    Show or set your university's Canvas address
  login     Open the app's Canvas sign-in window and wait for the session
  logout    Forget the saved session
  status    Whether the saved session still works
  setup     Store the credentials that let Oculus sign in without a browser
  auto      Sign in headlessly with the stored credentials, now
  forget    Forget the stored sign-in credentials
  diagnose  Report what the Okta sign-in page looks like, when `auto` fails
  ed        Show the Ed Discussion session status, or set a token manually
  help      Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s)

Options:
  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus auth canvas`

```
Show or set your university's Canvas address

Everything else is detected from it: how the university signs in, and whether automatic
sign-in (Okta only) is possible. The address cannot change while a library exists —
Start over in Settings → Storage first.

Usage: oculus auth canvas [ADDRESS]

Arguments:
  [ADDRESS]
          The address you open Canvas at, e.g. canvas.youruni.edu or
          youruni.instructure.com. Omit to show the current one

Options:
  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus auth login`

```
Open the app's Canvas sign-in window and wait for the session

Usage: oculus auth login

Options:
  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus auth logout`

```
Forget the saved session

Usage: oculus auth logout

Options:
  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus auth status`

```
Whether the saved session still works

Usage: oculus auth status

Options:
  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus auth setup`

```
Store the credentials that let Oculus sign in without a browser

Needs a TOTP factor (Google Authenticator) enrolled and its setup key. A code cannot be
derived from other codes, so the key must come from the enrolment screen — re-enrol the
factor if you never copied it.

Usage: oculus auth setup

Options:
  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus auth auto`

```
Sign in headlessly with the stored credentials, now

A manual sign-in: it skips the 10 min to 6 h wait between automatic attempts, but no two
attempts start within a minute, and three failed manual attempts in a row wait like
automatic ones. It cannot lift the pause a lockout or a rejected password leaves: fix
the credentials in the app (Settings → Canvas) or run `oculus auth setup`.

Usage: oculus auth auto

Options:
  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus auth forget`

```
Forget the stored sign-in credentials

Usage: oculus auth forget

Options:
  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus auth diagnose`

```
Report what the Okta sign-in page looks like, when `auto` fails

Usage: oculus auth diagnose

Options:
  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus auth ed`

```
Show the Ed Discussion session status, or set a token manually

Normally unnecessary — syncs mint the Ed session from the Canvas session via the
course's LTI launch. The manual token (DevTools → Network → any edstem /api request →
`x-token` header) is an override.

Usage: oculus auth ed [TOKEN]

Arguments:
  [TOKEN]
          An x-token JWT to save. Omit to check the current session

Options:
  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

## `oculus keyd`

```
Install, inspect or remove oculus-keyd, the credential broker

Usage: oculus keyd <COMMAND>

Commands:
  install    Install oculus-keyd on macOS; on Windows, open Oculus to start it
  status     Whether keyd is registered, current and answering
  uninstall  Stop keyd and remove its registration and stamp
  help       Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s)

Options:
  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus keyd install`

```
Install oculus-keyd on macOS; on Windows, open Oculus to start it

On macOS, a keyd whose signed helper app is nested in Oculus is registered in place; any
other has its helper app copied to `bin/` in the data dir first. Its LaunchAgent never
points into a build tree. Loading it reads no stored key.

On Windows, only the GUI starts the resident broker. This command cannot activate it;
open Oculus instead.

Usage: oculus keyd install [OPTIONS]

Options:
      --from <PATH>
          The signed keyd to install on macOS: its helper app or executable inside it.
          Defaults to this binary's bundled keyd, or, in a debug build, `bun run keyd`'s
          output

      --if-changed
          Do nothing when the installed keyd was built from the same source and its
          registration already runs it

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus keyd status`

```
Whether keyd is registered, current and answering

Sends keyd a `ping`. On macOS, this starts it if launchd has it loaded. On Windows, it
only checks the existing resident broker; open Oculus to start it. Never reads or prints
a stored key.

Usage: oculus keyd status

Options:
  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus keyd uninstall`

```
Stop keyd and remove its registration and stamp

On macOS, unloads its LaunchAgent and removes its copied helper app. On Windows, stops
the verified resident broker. The vault and its master key stay, so a reinstall finds
every stored key again.

Usage: oculus keyd uninstall

Options:
  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

## `oculus search`

```
Search the library by meaning (needs network and an API key).

The query is embedded by the same vision model that embedded every page image, so this
finds a slide about Lagrange multipliers when you ask for "constrained optimisation".
Embedding happens in the cloud, so this needs a network connection and the Voyage key
from Settings → Library; without either, and over an index that is empty or built by a
retired model, it fails loudly and points at `oculus grep`, which searches the same text
with no model at all.

Only PDF and Office pages are ranked here — Canvas pages, announcements and Ed threads
are markdown on disk and are covered by `oculus grep`.

Usage: oculus search [OPTIONS] <QUERY>

Arguments:
  <QUERY>
          What to look for, in plain language

Options:
  -s, --subject <SUBJECT_CODE>
          Restrict to one subject; prefix codes are fine (MULT20015)

  -n, --limit <LIMIT>
          How many pages to return (1-50)

          [default: 8]

      --full
          Print each hit's whole page instead of a one-line snippet

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

## `oculus grep`

```
Search the library by pattern (offline, no model).

Covers both halves of the library: the markdown on disk (Canvas pages, announcements,
assignments, Ed threads) and the page text of PDFs and spreadsheets, which lives in the
database — ripgrep over the library directory cannot see it, which is why this exists.

Needs no network and no model, so it is the fallback whenever `oculus search` cannot
run. The pattern is a regular expression by default and case-insensitive unless you ask
otherwise.

Usage: oculus grep [OPTIONS] <PATTERN>

Arguments:
  <PATTERN>
          Regular expression to look for

Options:
  -s, --subject <SUBJECT_CODE>
          Restrict to these subjects; prefix codes are fine. Repeatable

  -c, --category <CATEGORY>
          Only these categories (home, syllabus, upload, document, canvas, page,
          assignment, quiz, announcement, ed, lessons, file, module, image, other).
          Repeatable

  -F, --fixed
          Treat the pattern as literal text, not a regular expression

      --case-sensitive
          Match case exactly

  -l, --files-with-matches
          Print matching file paths only, one per line

  -n, --limit <LIMIT>
          Stop after this many matches

          [default: 40]

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

## `oculus read`

```
Print the text of one library file.

For a PDF or Office document this is the parsed page markdown from the database, so
`--pages` addresses the same page numbers `oculus search` and the app's viewer report. A
spreadsheet's text is one page per sheet, in workbook order. For markdown and other text
it is the file on disk. A PDF that has never been parsed says so rather than printing
nothing — run `oculus index <SUBJECT_CODE>` for it.

A notebook — a canvas with pages the student writes on, under `canvases/` — has no text.
It prints one line per page with the path of that page's picture, which the app redraws
a few seconds after each stroke, and how long ago; open the pictures with your image
tool. `--pages` picks pages by number. A whiteboard canvas has no pages and says so.

FILE may be a full library path, a bare filename, or any distinctive fragment of either.
An ambiguous fragment lists the candidates instead of guessing.

Usage: oculus read [OPTIONS] <FILE>

Arguments:
  <FILE>
          Library path, filename, or a fragment of either

Options:
  -p, --pages <RANGE>
          Pages to print: 12, 12-15, 12,14,20-22, or 30- for "30 to the end"

  -s, --subject <SUBJECT_CODE>
          Disambiguate by subject; prefix codes are fine

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

## `oculus files`

```
List the files in the library.

The `indexed` column is how many pages of a document are searchable; a PDF showing none
has not been parsed yet.

Usage: oculus files [OPTIONS] [SUBJECT_CODE]...

Arguments:
  [SUBJECT_CODE]...
          Subjects to list. Omit for every subject

Options:
  -t, --type <EXT>
          Only this extension (pdf, md, pptx, docx, png …)

  -c, --category <CATEGORY>
          Only these categories (home, syllabus, upload, document, canvas, page,
          assignment, quiz, announcement, ed, lessons, file, module, image, other).
          Repeatable

  -m, --match <TEXT>
          Only paths containing this text (case-insensitive)

      --indexed
          Only files with pages in the retrieval index

  -n, --limit <LIMIT>
          Stop after this many files

          [default: 200]

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

```
Plan work: projects, their boards, and what is on them

Usage: oculus project <COMMAND>

Commands:
  list    List projects and how far along they are
  show    Show one project: its brief, its board, and every task on it
  events  List calendar events that a project can link to, including past events
  create  Create a project
  update  Change a project's name, subject, dates, brief, tags, calendar link or status
```

### `oculus project list`

```
List projects and how far along they are.

Active projects only, unless `--archived`. Each line starts with the id every other
project and task command takes, and ends with finished/total tasks.

Usage: oculus project list [OPTIONS]

Options:
  -s, --subject <SUBJECT_CODE>
          Only this subject's projects; prefix codes are fine (COMP30026)

      --personal
          Only projects belonging to no subject

      --archived
          Archived projects instead of active ones

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus project show`

```
Show one project: its brief, its board, and every task on it.

Tasks are printed under their column in the board's own order, subtasks indented under
their parent. The bracketed name after each column heading is the column **id** — that
is what `--column` takes.

Usage: oculus project show <ID>

Arguments:
  <ID>
          Project id, as `oculus project list` prints it

Options:
  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus project events`

```
List calendar events that a project can link to, including past events.

Includes Canvas events, personal calendar notes and fallback lectures, with the same ids
the app uses. Tasks are excluded. Pass an id to --event.

Usage: oculus project events [OPTIONS]

Options:
  -s, --subject <SUBJECT_CODE>
          Only this subject's events; omit for every subject and personal events

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus project create`

```
Create a project.

It opens with the app's default board — `backlog`, `todo`, `doing`, `done` — and no
tasks; `oculus task add --batch` is how a breakdown goes in. Rows written by this binary
are marked `source: agent`, so the board can show what it did not write itself.

Prints the new project's id.

Usage: oculus project create [OPTIONS] <NAME>

Arguments:
  <NAME>
          What the project is called

Options:
  -s, --subject <SUBJECT_CODE>
          Scope it to a subject; prefix codes are fine (COMP30026), and the current term
          wins a tie. Omit for a personal project

      --due <ISO>
          When the whole thing is due, ISO 8601 (2026-09-20T23:59:00Z)

      --starts <ISO>
          When work on it starts, ISO 8601

      --brief <TEXT>
          Markdown About text; use --brief-file for multiple lines

      --brief-file <FILE>
          Read Markdown About text from a UTF-8 file, or - for stdin

      --event <ID>
          Link a calendar event by the id printed by project events

      --tags <TAGS>
          Comma-separated labels for the About page (report,group,week-5)

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus project update`

```
Change a project's name, subject, dates, brief, tags, calendar link or status.

Only the flags you pass are written; everything else is left alone. Pass an **empty
string** to clear a field: `--due ""` takes the due date off.

`--status archived` is how a project leaves the board without being deleted; its tasks
stay and `--status active` brings it back.

Usage: oculus project update [OPTIONS] <ID>

Arguments:
  <ID>
          Project id

Options:
      --name <NAME>
          Rename it

  -s, --subject <SUBJECT_CODE>
          Move the project to this subject; its tasks follow

      --personal
          Make the project personal (clear its subject)

      --due <ISO>
          Due date, ISO 8601, or "" to clear

      --starts <ISO>
          Start date, ISO 8601, or "" to clear

      --brief <TEXT>
          Replace the brief, or "" to clear it

      --brief-file <FILE>
          Read Markdown About text from a UTF-8 file, or - for stdin; empty clears

      --event <ID>
          Link a calendar event (project events lists ids), or "" to unlink

      --status <STATUS>
          active or archived

          [possible values: active, archived]

      --tags <TAGS>
          Replace every tag with this comma-separated list, or "" to clear them. There
          is no add/remove: the whole set is written at once, the same way the About
          page's editor writes it

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

## `oculus task`

```
Add, move, refile, finish and delete tasks, on a board or on none

Usage: oculus task <COMMAND>

Commands:
  list    List tasks — one project's, or every task there is
  show    Show a task's full Markdown notes, properties, subtasks and related files
  add     Add one task, or a whole breakdown in one call
  update  Change a task's title, notes, dates, estimate, tags or attached files
  move    Move a task to another column, or reorder it within one
  refile  File a task under another project, or under none at all
  rm      Delete a task, and its subtasks with it
  help    Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s)

Options:
  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus task list`

```
List tasks — one project's, or every task there is.

Grouped by column in the board's order, subtasks under their parent. A task sitting in a
`done` column carries the time it landed there.

Without `-p` this spans **every** project and includes the tasks that belong to none,
printed as one board per project under its name, with the unfiled ones first.
`--unfiled` lists only those: the pile with no board of its own, which is the one that
needs looking at.

A task's tags follow its title as `#Name`, then its due date, estimate and how many
library files are attached (`2 files`). `--tag` keeps only the tasks carrying one tag.

Usage: oculus task list [OPTIONS]

Options:
  -p, --project <ID>
          Which project (omit for every task in the library)

      --unfiled
          Only tasks that belong to no project at all

  -c, --column <ID>
          Only this board column (its id, e.g. todo) — needs --project, since a column
          id only means something against one board

      --due-before <ISO>
          Only tasks due before this ISO 8601 timestamp. Compared as text, so pass the
          same shape the dates were written in (UTC, usually)

      --tag <NAME>
          Only tasks with this tag (its name, any case; `oculus tag list` has them)

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus task show`

```
Show a task's full Markdown notes, properties, subtasks and related files

Usage: oculus task show <ID>

Arguments:
  <ID>
          Task id

Options:
  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus task add`

```
Add one task, or a whole breakdown in one call.

**Without `-p` the task belongs to no project at all** — the same thing the app's Tasks
page writes by default, and the answer to "write this down, I have not decided where it
goes". That is the absence of a project, not a project called Inbox, so nothing needs
cleaning up if it is never filed; `oculus task refile` files it later. Its board is the
default one (`backlog`, `todo`, `doing`, `done`), so filing it into a project created by
this binary needs no translation.

A task lands at the end of its column; without `--column` that is the first column of
its board. The column id is checked against that board and an unknown one is refused,
listing the ids it does have — a task filed under a column that does not exist is drawn
by nothing, in any view. Landing in a `done` column marks the task finished, exactly as
moving it there would.

`--parent` makes the task a subtask. Subtasks are one level deep: a subtask cannot
itself be given children.

`--tags "Assignment,Exam"` tags it by name, ignoring case; a name the registry (`oculus
tag list`) lacks is created on the spot in the default colour. `--file PATH`
(repeatable) attaches a library file by the path `oculus files` prints; a path that
matches no file, or more than one, is refused.

BREAKDOWNS: `--batch -` reads a JSON array of tasks from stdin (or a file, `--batch
tasks.json`) and writes them in one call — use it for anything past two or three:

[{"title":"Read the brief","column":"todo","due":"2026-09-20T23:59:00Z"},
{"title":"Outline","key":"outline"}, {"title":"Draft intro","parent":"outline"}]

Per task: `title` (required), `column`, `body`, `due`, `starts`, `estimate` (minutes),
`tags` (an array of tag names), `files` (an array of library paths), `parent`, `key`.
`parent` is either an existing task's id (a number) or the `key` of an **earlier task in
the same batch**, which is how a parent and its subtasks go in together. `key` is never
stored. An unknown field is an error rather than a silent no-op.

The batch is **all or nothing**: one transaction, so a bad item — unknown column, a
parent that is already a subtask, a date that is not a date — writes none of them and
says which item failed. Fix it and re-send; it can never leave half a breakdown on the
board.

Prints the new task ids in the order they were given.

Usage: oculus task add [OPTIONS] [TITLE]

Arguments:
  [TITLE]
          The task's title. Omit when using --batch

Options:
  -p, --project <ID>
          Which project (omit to file it nowhere)

  -c, --column <ID>
          Board column id (default: the first column of its board)

      --parent <TASK_ID>
          Make this a subtask of that task id

      --due <ISO>
          Due date, ISO 8601

      --starts <ISO>
          Start date, ISO 8601

      --estimate <MIN>
          How long you think it will take, in minutes

      --body <TEXT>
          Markdown notes; use --body-file for multiple lines

      --body-file <FILE>
          Read Markdown notes from a UTF-8 file, or - for stdin

      --tags <NAMES>
          Comma-separated tag names (Assignment,Exam); new names are created

      --file <PATH>
          Attach a library file by its relative path; repeat for several

      --batch <FILE>
          Read a JSON array of tasks from stdin (-) or a file

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus task update`

```
Change a task's title, notes, dates, estimate, tags or attached files.

Only the flags you pass are written. Pass an **empty string** to clear a field: `--due
""`, `--estimate ""`, `--tags ""`.

`--tags "A,B"` **replaces** the whole tag set (names, any case; unknown ones are
created). `--attach PATH` and `--detach PATH` add or remove one library file by the path
`oculus files` prints, and may be repeated; attaching a file already attached, or
detaching one that is not, changes nothing.

Where a task *sits* is not here: column, order and done-ness are one fact, and `oculus
task move` is their only writer — it is the command that reads the board to learn
whether the destination column means finished.

Usage: oculus task update [OPTIONS] <ID>

Arguments:
  <ID>
          Task id

Options:
      --title <TEXT>
          Rename it

      --body <TEXT>
          Replace the notes, or "" to clear

      --body-file <FILE>
          Read Markdown notes from a UTF-8 file, or - for stdin; empty clears

      --due <ISO>
          Due date, ISO 8601, or "" to clear

      --starts <ISO>
          Start date, ISO 8601, or "" to clear

      --estimate <MIN>
          Minutes, or "" to clear

      --tags <NAMES>
          Replace every tag with this comma-separated list of names, or "" to clear them

      --attach <PATH>
          Attach a library file by its relative path; repeat for several

      --detach <PATH>
          Detach a library file by its relative path; repeat for several

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus task move`

```
Move a task to another column, or reorder it within one.

This is also how a task is finished: landing in a column whose kind is `done` stamps it,
and leaving one clears that again. The column's *kind* decides, not its name — which is
why there is no `--done` flag anywhere.

Without `--after` or `--before` the task goes to the end of the column. Both name tasks
already in the destination column: `--after 12` puts it straight below task 12,
`--before 12` straight above it.

Usage: oculus task move [OPTIONS] --column <ID> <ID>

Arguments:
  <ID>
          Task id

Options:
  -c, --column <ID>
          Destination column id (e.g. done)

      --after <TASK_ID>
          Put it directly below this task

      --before <TASK_ID>
          Put it directly above this task

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus task refile`

```
File a task under another project, or under none at all.

The one command that changes which project a task belongs to. It takes the task's
**subtasks with it** — a subtask sits in its parent's project, so there is no honest
half of this move, and a subtask on its own is refused and names its parent instead.

The column maps across by *kind*: a task in a column that means "in flight" lands in the
**first** column of that kind on the destination's board, so entering a kind puts you at
its start. A board with no column of that kind — no Done column for a finished task — is
refused rather than given the nearest one; there is no nearest kind. Whether the task is
finished follows the column it lands in, as it does everywhere else.

It lands at the **end** of that column: `position` is an order inside one project's
column and means nothing across two, so there is no slot in the destination to aim at.
`oculus task move` is how it is then placed.

Usage: oculus task refile [OPTIONS] <ID>

Arguments:
  <ID>
          Task id

Options:
  -p, --project <ID>
          File it under this project

      --unfiled
          Take it out of every project instead

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus task rm`

```
Delete a task, and its subtasks with it.

There is no undo, and nothing else cleans these up — a task that is merely finished
belongs in a `done` column (`oculus task move`), not deleted.

Usage: oculus task rm <ID>

Arguments:
  <ID>
          Task id

Options:
  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

## `oculus memory`

```
Read and write the memory store the agents keep in the library

Usage: oculus memory <COMMAND>

Commands:
  list     What is already known, as the index shows it
  read     Print one memory in full
  write    Write a memory — front matter, dates and index included
  rm       Delete a memory that turned out to be wrong
  move     File a memory under a different bucket
  reindex  Rebuild a bucket's `MEMORY.md` from the files in it
  promote  Turn a memory into a standing preference in `TASTE.md`
  help     Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s)

Options:
  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus memory list`

```
What is already known, as the index shows it.

Read this before answering, not after: it is a few hundred bytes and it is the only
thing that carries between conversations. Without `-s` it lists the cross-subject
bucket; `--all` walks every bucket there is.

Each line leads with the **name**, which is what `read`, `rm`, `move` and `--link` take,
and what a second `write` under updates rather than duplicates. Its one-line description
follows underneath.

Usage: oculus memory list [OPTIONS]

Options:
  -s, --subject <CODE>
          Only this subject's memories (a code, e.g. INFO30006)

      --all
          Every bucket: across subjects, then one per course

      --type <TYPE>
          Only memories of this type

          [possible values: user, feedback, project, reference]

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus memory read`

```
Print one memory in full.

The name is the file's, without `.md` — `memory list` prints it. A close-enough spelling
finds it anyway: the hyphens need not fall where the filename puts them, the title works
in place of the name, and a prefix or a distinctive fragment works when only one memory
answers to it. Both buckets are searched unless `-s` narrows it.

Usage: oculus memory read [OPTIONS] <NAME>

Arguments:
  <NAME>
          Which memory

Options:
  -s, --subject <CODE>
          Look only in this subject's bucket

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus memory write`

```
Write a memory — front matter, dates and index included.

**This is the way to remember something, rather than writing the markdown by hand.** A
memory is two files — the fact, and a line in that folder's `MEMORY.md` — and the second
is the one that gets skipped, which is the one that decides whether the next
conversation ever opens the first. Here the index is rewritten from the files every
time, so it cannot go stale, and the front matter is built from the flags: pass the fact
and how it is filed, and `name`, `created`, `updated` and the index are not yours to
remember.

**Filing is `-s` or nothing.** A fact that names one subject takes `-s <CODE>` and lands
in that subject's bucket — always, including when it came up in a conversation scoped to
nothing. Without `-s` it goes in the cross-subject bucket, which is for the student
themselves and for what spans subjects.

**A name that is already filed is updated, not duplicated**, keeping its `created` date
and anything this call leaves out. That is what makes the store a record of what is true
rather than a log of what was said.

The body is one line as `--text`, or a file with `--body` (`-` for stdin) — the shell an
in-app agent runs through refuses a newline inside an argument, so anything with
paragraphs in it is written to a file first.

oculus memory write --type reference --about "Ed answers are the marking authority for
INFO30006; the brief is not" --text "Staff said in Ed #66 that everything in lectures
and tutorials is assessable." -s INFO30006

oculus memory write tchan-study-workflow --type feedback --about "Wants a verdict then
the evidence, never a survey of options" --text "Triages by return on investment and
does the arithmetic before asking." --why "He is asking for the missing evidence, not to
be told what to do." --how "Lead with one recommendation, then the specific evidence
under it."

Usage: oculus memory write [OPTIONS] [NAME]

Arguments:
  [NAME]
          The file's name. Omit and it is taken from --about — but **name it to update
          it**: a write that derives a name from a changed line is a new memory, the
          same as it would be for any other file

Options:
  -s, --subject <CODE>
          File it under this subject (omit for the cross-subject bucket)

      --about <TEXT>
          The one line the index shows — what a reader sees before opening it

          [alias: --description]

      --type <TYPE>
          What kind of memory this is

          [possible values: user, feedback, project, reference]

      --title <TEXT>
          What the index calls it (default: the name, read back as words)

      --text <TEXT>
          The fact itself, on one line

      --body <FILE>
          The fact, from a file — or `-` for stdin

      --why <TEXT>
          Why it is true, or why it matters. Required for feedback and project

      --how <TEXT>
          What a later session should do about it. Required for feedback and project

      --source <TEXT>
          Where the fact came from — a library path, an Ed number, a lecture

      --link <NAME>
          Another memory this one bears on, by name. Repeatable

      --meta <K=V>
          Any other front-matter field, as key=value. Repeatable

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus memory rm`

```
Delete a memory that turned out to be wrong.

The store is what is true, not what was said, so a fact that has been overtaken is
deleted rather than left to be read again. **There is no undo** — nothing upstream has a
copy of this, the way a course file comes back on the next sync. The index is rewritten
without it.

Usage: oculus memory rm [OPTIONS] <NAME>

Arguments:
  <NAME>
          Which memory

Options:
  -s, --subject <CODE>
          Look only in this subject's bucket

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus memory move`

```
File a memory under a different bucket.

For the mistake the two buckets exist to make visible: a fact about one subject that
ended up in the cross-subject store, or the reverse. The file moves whole — body, dates
and all — and both indexes are rewritten, which is the part that made this worth a
command rather than a delete and a retype.

Usage: oculus memory move [OPTIONS] <NAME>

Arguments:
  <NAME>
          Which memory

Options:
  -s, --subject <CODE>
          File it under this subject

      --global
          File it across subjects instead

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus memory reindex`

```
Rebuild a bucket's `MEMORY.md` from the files in it.

Every write does this already, so it is here for the store as it stands today: memories
written by hand before this command existed, or a file dropped in from somewhere.
Whatever prose sits above the generated list is kept.

Usage: oculus memory reindex [OPTIONS]

Options:
  -s, --subject <CODE>
          Only this subject's bucket

      --all
          Every bucket there is

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus memory promote`

```
Turn a memory into a standing preference in `TASTE.md`.

The second half of the rule that file states: the first time something is said about how
work should be done it is a `feedback` memory, and when it comes up again it earns a
line in `TASTE.md` and the memory goes. This does both ends of that in one call, so the
promotion is not a hand-edit nobody makes.

Usage: oculus memory promote [OPTIONS] --section <NAME> <NAME>

Arguments:
  <NAME>
          Which memory

Options:
      --section <NAME>
          Which heading it belongs under

          [possible values: writing, working, study]

      --as <TEXT>
          The bullet, written as an instruction (default: the memory's own line)

      --keep
          Leave the memory in place instead of deleting it

  -s, --subject <CODE>
          Look only in this subject's bucket

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

## `oculus lecture`

```
Look inside a downloaded lecture recording

Usage: oculus lecture <COMMAND>

Commands:
  candidates  Find where a recording plausibly changes topic
  chapters    Name a recording's chapters with a CLI agent, and store them
  end         Find where a recording's lecture ends, before its Q&A and dead air
  help        Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s)

Options:
  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus lecture candidates`

```
Find where a recording plausibly changes topic

Samples the video one frame a second and reports the moments the picture changes hard
enough to be a new slide, thinned so no two are within 90 seconds. A transcript silence
near a change nudges its score up; it never creates a boundary on its own.

Detection is a single ffmpeg decode — a few seconds for an hour of video — so nothing is
stored and re-running always reflects the file on disk. This is the raw candidate set:
no titles and no summaries, which are a later stage's job.

Usage: oculus lecture candidates [OPTIONS] <LECTURE_ID>

Arguments:
  <LECTURE_ID>
          Lecture id, as `oculus list -l` prints it; a unique prefix is enough

Options:
      --frames
          Also write one JPEG per candidate into the lecture's `frames/` folder, so the
          boundaries can be checked by eye

      --source <N>
          Which captured stream to read — 1 or 2. Default: source 1, unless it turns out
          to be dead, in which case source 2 if it is downloaded

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus lecture chapters`

```
Name a recording's chapters with a CLI agent, and store them

Detects the boundary candidates, grabs a frame for each, then hands the list, the
transcript and the frames folder to a coding agent and asks it which of them are real
topic changes. The agent replies with JSON; this command validates it against the
candidate set and writes the rows. The agent never touches the database.

One bad chapter rejects the whole set: a chapter list is a shape, and a missing chapter
is not a gap but twenty minutes silently attributed to the chapter before it.

Usage: oculus lecture chapters [OPTIONS] <LECTURE_ID>

Arguments:
  <LECTURE_ID>
          Lecture id, as `oculus list -l` prints it; a unique prefix is enough

Options:
  -p, --provider <PROVIDER>
          Which CLI to drive (default: the configured one)

          [possible values: claude, codex, opencode]

  -m, --model <MODEL>
          Model to request (default: the configured one)

      --effort <EFFORT>
          Reasoning effort — low, medium, high, xhigh, max (default: the configured one)

      --force
          Re-run over a lecture that already has chapters, replacing them

      --source <N>
          Which captured stream to read — 1 or 2. Default: source 1, unless it turns out
          to be dead, in which case source 2 if it is downloaded

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus lecture end`

```
Find where a recording's lecture ends, before its Q&A and dead air

Recordings run on after the lecturer signs off — students at the lectern, packing up, a
black projector — and the microphone keeps transcribing. This hands the last 15 minutes
of the transcript to a model in one short turn with no tools, and asks which line the
lecturer finishes on. The model cites that line's second and quotes it; both are checked
against the transcript, and a reply that fails is asked again once with the reason. A
recording cut off mid-lecture has no end, and is stored as such.

If the recording is downloaded, its last 15 minutes are decoded too: a projector that
goes black for good is mentioned to the model as a hint, never applied on its own. Only
the transcript is required.

The end stored is the end of the line the quote finishes in. A lecture already watched
to within 10 seconds of it is marked done.

Usage: oculus lecture end [OPTIONS] <LECTURE_ID|--all>

Arguments:
  [LECTURE_ID]...
          Lecture ids, as `oculus list -l` prints them; a unique prefix is enough

Options:
      --all
          Every lecture with a transcript whose end has not been looked for (with
          --force, every lecture with a transcript)

  -p, --provider <PROVIDER>
          Which CLI to drive (default: the configured one)

          [possible values: claude, codex, opencode]

  -m, --model <MODEL>
          Model to request (default: the configured one)

      --effort <EFFORT>
          Reasoning effort — low, medium, high, xhigh, max (default: the configured one)

      --force
          Re-run over a lecture whose end is already found, replacing it

      --dry-run
          Ask and print, but write nothing — not the end, not the status, not done

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

## `oculus transcribe`

```
Transcribe a video that has no captions, on Groq or on this Mac

Extracts the video's audio, transcribes it, and writes the timed text beside the video
as `<video>.vtt` — `Week 1.mp4` gets `Week 1.mp4.vtt`. Three engines, tried in the order
set in Settings → Transcription — Groq, local Whisper, then on-device speech unless
changed there — and one switched off there is skipped. Whisper on Groq's free tier needs
a Groq API key saved in Settings (the audio is uploaded, split into parts by time when
it is too large for one upload); local Whisper needs a model downloaded there; Apple's
on-device speech recognition needs macOS 26 or later. Both local engines are free and
keep the audio on this Mac. Every engine transcribes in the language set there, English
by default.

Groq's free tier caps how many seconds of audio it takes an hour and a day; past that
the run moves on to the next engine, or, with no engine left, fails and says when to try
again. Any other failure ends the run. Nothing is written unless every part comes back,
and nothing is recorded in the database.

Usage: oculus transcribe [OPTIONS] <VIDEO>

Arguments:
  <VIDEO>
          A video inside the library: absolute, relative to this directory, or relative
          to the library root

Options:
      --engine <ENGINE>
          Use only this engine, with no fallback (default: the first in the Settings
          order that answers)

          [possible values: groq, whisper, apple]

      --force
          Transcribe again when the `.vtt` already exists, replacing it

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

## `oculus studio`

```
Make, render, check and narrate Studio videos: TSX scenes drawn frame by frame

Usage: oculus studio <COMMAND>

Commands:
  new         Make a new video under `<app data>/studio/videos/<SLUG>/`
  list        List the videos under `<app data>/studio/videos/`
  frame       Render one frame of a video to a PNG
  strip       Render frames across a stretch of a video as one contact-sheet PNG
  lint        Check a whole video, or one scene, without writing to its folder
  brief       Print one scene builder's whole input
  beats       Print what changes on screen in one scene, as a timeline
  gallery     Render every example of a component as a still
  slide       Crop a region of a library PDF page into a video's assets
  blocks      List a parsed PDF's blocks: what `slide` can crop
  components  List, show, promote or seed a video's components
  themes      Promote a video's own theme file into a library
  render      Render a video to an mp4
  narrate     Synthesise and time a video's narration, writing narration/manifest.json
  tts         Synthesise one clip of text to a WAV, to hear a voice
  g2p         Show how Kokoro reads text: each word's phonemes and who read it
  pronounce   Suggest how Kokoro should say a word, for the student to review
  voices      List Kokoro's voices, or download or delete them and its packs
  agents      Which models a chat agent's Studio subagents run on, and how to start one
  aligner     Download, check or delete the narration aligner model (378 MB)
  help        Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s)

Options:
  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus studio new`

```
Make a new video under `<app data>/studio/videos/<SLUG>/`

Writes `video.json` (1920x1080, or 1080x1920 with `--portrait`, 30 fps, the default
theme, the subject, and one silent `TitleCard` scene holding `--title`), an empty
`script.md`, and empty `components/` and `assets/`, then prints the folder. The default
theme is the `defaultTheme` in the subject library's `library.json`, else the global
library's, else `default`, and video.json names it. Every other `oculus studio` command
takes the slug in place of the folder. Refuses a slug that exists.

oculus studio new gradient-descent --subject COMP30027 --title "Gradient descent"

Usage: oculus studio new [OPTIONS] <SLUG>

Arguments:
  <SLUG>
          The video's name: lowercase letters, digits and `-`

Options:
      --subject <CODE>
          The course the video belongs to; its library is read before the global one

      --title <TITLE>
          The title card's text (default: the slug, spaced)

      --portrait
          1080x1920 instead of 1920x1080

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus studio list`

```
List the videos under `<app data>/studio/videos/`

One line per video: its slug, subject, scene count, whether it has narration
(`narrated`; `lint` says whether it is current), the renders in its `renders/` and when
it last changed. A folder whose video.json does not load is listed with the reason.

Usage: oculus studio list [OPTIONS]

Options:
      --subject <CODE>
          Only this course's videos

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus studio frame`

```
Render one frame of a video to a PNG

A video is a folder: `video.json` (size, theme and the scenes in order, each a
component, its props and how many seconds it holds), `components/<Name>.tsx` (one TSX
component per file, run in a sandbox), `assets/` (the images `<Image src>` names) and,
for a narrated video, `script.md` and `narration/manifest.json`, which make a narrated
scene last as long as its narration. Every frame is a pure function of the folder and
the time, so the same call always draws the same pixels.

Time is either global, `--t` seconds from the start of the video, or scene-relative,
`--scene N --at S` (scenes count from 0). With neither it draws the first frame. The PNG
goes to `<DIR>/out/frame-<t>.png`, `t` global, unless `-o` names another file. Anything
a component passes to `console.log` is printed after the path.

oculus studio frame lectures/week-4 --t 12.4

oculus studio frame lectures/week-4 --scene 2 --at 0.5 -o /tmp/check.png --scale 0.5

Usage: oculus studio frame [OPTIONS] <DIR>

Arguments:
  <DIR>
          The video folder, the one holding `video.json` (or its slug)

Options:
      --t <SECONDS>
          Seconds from the start of the video (default: 0)

      --scene <N>
          Which scene, counting from 0; the time is then `--at` within it

      --at <SECONDS>
          Seconds from the start of `--scene` (default: 0)

  -o, --out <OUT.png>
          Where to write the PNG (default: `<DIR>/out/frame-<t>.png`)

      --scale <F>
          Pixel scale over the same layout: 0.5 draws a 1080p video at 540p

          [default: 1]

      --motion-blur
          Average sub-frames over a 180° shutter at the video's fps, as many as the
          motion needs (off unless given, whatever the theme's motionBlur says)

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus studio strip`

```
Render frames across a stretch of a video as one contact-sheet PNG

Draws `--n` frames evenly spaced from `--from` to `--to` (both included, global
seconds), tiled `--cols` a row, each labelled under the frame with its time and, in a
video of several scenes, its scene and the time within it. It is how to check a motion
without a video: what moves, in which order, and where it settles. `--scene N` covers
that scene alone. A `--to` at or past the end is the video's last moment.

Frames render in parallel, one renderer per thread (default half the cores, capped to
keep memory under 2 GB); the sheet is the same at any thread count. A frame that fails
fails the sheet, naming its time and scene. The PNG goes to
`<DIR>/out/strip-<from>-<to>.png` unless `-o` names another file.

oculus studio strip lectures/week-4

oculus studio strip lectures/week-4 --scene 2 --n 8 --cols 8 --scale 0.2

oculus studio strip lectures/week-4 --from 3 --to 4 --n 6 -o /tmp/motion.png

Usage: oculus studio strip [OPTIONS] <DIR>

Arguments:
  <DIR>
          The video folder, the one holding `video.json` (or its slug)

Options:
      --from <SECONDS>
          First frame, in seconds from the start of the video (default: 0)

      --to <SECONDS>
          Last frame, in seconds from the start of the video (default: the end)

      --scene <N>
          Cover only this scene, counting from 0

      --n <K>
          How many frames

          [default: 12]

      --cols <C>
          Frames per row

          [default: 4]

      --scale <F>
          Each frame's scale over the video's size: 0.25 makes 480x270 tiles of a 1080p
          video

          [default: 0.25]

      --threads <T>
          Render threads (default: half the cores, at most one per frame)

      --motion-blur
          Blur each frame over a 180° shutter at the video's fps (see `frame --help`)

  -o, --out <OUT.png>
          Where to write the PNG (default: `<DIR>/out/strip-<from>-<to>.png`)

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus studio lint`

```
Check a whole video, or one scene, without writing to its folder

Loads every component the video uses, checks each scene's props and each component's
`examples` against its `props` schema, and renders every scene at its first and last
moment. For a narrated video it also checks `script.md` (sections no scene matches, text
not written as it is said) and the narration (missing or stale clips, unscripted
speech). When the video narrates with Kokoro it also reads every section as `narrate`
will: a missing `g2p-en-us` pack, a lexicon entry that is not valid, a word with no
phonemes or a sentence too long for Kokoro is an error.

Each scene that renders is then laid out every 0.2 s and at each cue word (never
painted) for warnings: a node past the frame's edge (`off_frame`), narration over a
frame where nothing changes for more than 2.5 s or an empty opening (`still`),
everything kept small in one half of the frame for more than 3 s (`half_frame`), and a
Math down to a piece or two, or a tiny mark alone, at the end (`fragment`). Each names
its time span and the words said in it.

Three levels: `error` (exits 1, so it can gate a render), `warning` and `note` (a word
the aligner was unsure of, a word Kokoro's guesser read); warnings and notes never
change the exit code. Errors print one a line in full; repeats of a warning or note in
one scene print as one line with a count and the first few. `--json` gives one entry per
issue with its `level`.

See `oculus studio frame --help` for what a video folder holds.

oculus studio lint shor --scene mod

Usage: oculus studio lint [OPTIONS] <DIR>

Arguments:
  <DIR>
          The video folder, the one holding `video.json` (or its slug)

Options:
      --scene <ID|N>
          Only this scene (its id in video.json, or its index counting from 0), with its
          component and the video settings it renders with

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus studio brief`

```
Print one scene builder's whole input

For one scene: its index, component and props; the scenes before and after it, whether
their components exist yet, and what their storyboard entries say under `Carries in:`
and `Hands on:`; its own `storyboard.md` entry verbatim (from its `### <id>` heading to
the next heading or `---`); the `notes/` files the entry names, else every file in
`notes/`; its narration, one line per sentence, each word with the time `word()` returns
for it (scene seconds, the theme's lead included) and each pause after its word at the
time `pause()` returns; and the exact `strip`, `frame` and `gallery` calls that check
it, `-o` paths absolute. Stale or missing narration prints its error and the script text
instead. Reads only the folder.

oculus studio brief shor --scene squares

oculus studio brief lectures/week-4 --scene 3 --json
```

### `oculus studio beats`

```
Print what changes on screen in one scene, as a timeline

Lays the scene out every 0.2 s and at each cue word (never painted) and lists, per key
(or per Math, or per TSX line for nodes with no key near them), when it appears,
vanishes, moves (centre more than 8 px), resizes, recolours or is rewritten, each with
the words said then, and each `[pause]` with its length. Numbered keys doing the same
thing at the same moment share a line (`d12-d14`). A builder checks a beat table against
it as text instead of reading a strip. At most 80 lines print; `--json` gives every beat
as `{index, id, component, length, beats: [{t, end, event, who, detail, words}]}`.

oculus studio beats shor --scene squares
```

### `oculus studio gallery`

```
Render every example of a component as a still

Each entry of the component's `examples` is drawn as one PNG, at one moment: `--t`
seconds from the start of the component's scene, by default its middle. That is the
middle of the first scene that uses it when the scene is silent with a `hold`, else of a
6 s preview (a narrated scene's length needs its narration, which a gallery never reads,
so it runs before `narrate`; `word()` throws in a gallery). Examples render in parallel
and the PNGs are the same at any thread count. The component is read through the cascade
(the video's `components/`, then the subject's library, then the global one), and the
theme the same way. `--sheet` also writes all the stills as one contact sheet, `--cols`
a row. Stills are named `<Component>-<example>.png`.

oculus studio gallery lectures/week-4 Bars

oculus studio gallery lectures/week-4 Bars --subject COMP2011 --sheet --cols 2

Usage: oculus studio gallery [OPTIONS] <DIR> <COMPONENT>

Arguments:
  <DIR>
          The video folder, the one holding `video.json` (or its slug)

  <COMPONENT>
          The component's name (PascalCase), as its file is named

Options:
      --subject <CODE>
          The course whose library is read for this load, over video.json's

      --theme <THEME>
          The theme (a bundled or library name, or a `.json` path), over video.json's

      --t <SECONDS>
          Seconds from the start of the component's scene (default: the middle of its
          silent scene's hold, or 3 s of the 6 s preview)

      --out <DIR>
          The folder for the PNGs (default: `<DIR>/out/gallery/`)

      --sheet
          Also write every still as one contact sheet, `<Component>.png`

      --cols <N>
          Stills per row in the contact sheet

          [default: 4]

      --threads <T>
          Render threads (default: half the cores, at most one per example)

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus studio slide`

```
Crop a region of a library PDF page into a video's assets

Renders the region with the app's PDF renderer and writes
`<DIR>/assets/slides/<NAME>.png` (sharp at up to 2x the video's frame),
`<NAME>.page.png` (the whole page fitted to the frame, for a zoom in from the page) and
`<NAME>.json`: the PDF's library path and sha256, the page, the crop as fractions of the
page, how it was chosen, the blocks inside it as fractions of the crop (kind and text,
for highlight boxes), and the props for the `Slide` starter, which it also prints. FILE
resolves as for `oculus read`. Name the region one way: `--find` text in a block (a
figure, chart or table that holds it wins over running text; a caption that is its own
block brings the figure beside it; a tie or no match lists the candidates), `--block`
indices from `oculus studio blocks`, or `--bbox`. Blocks come from the parse record, so
`--find` and `--block` need a parsed PDF. No edge slices ink: where the box cuts a line
(a caption under a figure's box) the edge moves out to take it in, up to 6% of the page;
a caption or label in the margin joins a figure, other text there is left out; the
sidecar's `edges` says what moved, and `--exact` keeps the box as given. The same inputs
write the same bytes; lint warns when the PDF changes after.

oculus studio slide momentum lecture-04.pdf --find "Figure 3" --name descent

oculus studio slide momentum lecture-04.pdf --page 12 --block 3,4

oculus studio slide momentum lecture-04.pdf --page 12 --bbox 0.5,0.2,0.95,0.8

Usage: oculus studio slide [OPTIONS] <DIR> <FILE>

Arguments:
  <DIR>
          The video folder, the one holding `video.json` (or its slug)

  <FILE>
          Library path, filename, or a fragment of either

Options:
  -p, --page <N>
          The page, from 1 (needed by --block and --bbox; --find without it searches
          every page)

      --find <TEXT>
          Text in the block to crop, any case, e.g. "Figure 3"

      --block <I[,J…]>
          Block indices on the page; several are cropped as one region round them all

      --bbox <X0,Y0,X1,Y1>
          A box as fractions of the page from its top left

      --name <NAME>
          The files' name under assets/slides/ (default: from the page and what was
          asked, e.g. `p12-figure-3`)

      --pad <FRACTION>
          Margin round the region, as a fraction of the page's shorter side

          [default: 0.02]

      --width <PX>
          The crop's width in pixels (default: 2x what fills the frame, at most 6
          megapixels)

      --replace
          Overwrite a slide of the same name cropped from another PDF

      --exact
          Keep the padded box as it is; by default each edge moves off any ink it would
          cut (out over a caption, back before other text)

  -s, --subject <SUBJECT_CODE>
          Disambiguate FILE by subject; prefix codes are fine

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

```
List, show, promote or seed a video's components

data>/studio/subjects/<CODE>/ components/`) or `global` (`<app
data>/studio/library/components/`). `promote` copies one of the video's own components
into a library. `seed` copies the starter set into the global library; it never replaces
```

### `oculus studio render`

```
Render a video to an mp4

Each scene is rendered frame by frame (in parallel, one renderer per thread) and encoded
by ffmpeg as its own segment, which is kept in `<DIR>/.cache/segments/` under a hash of
everything its frames depend on: the scene and the one before it, their narration, the
theme, the `components/` and `assets/` folders and the render settings. A second render
only renders the scenes an edit touched and prints `cached` for the rest. The segments
are joined without re-encoding, beside the narration clips mixed into one track (AAC).
Segments no preset's last render used are deleted afterwards.

The preset says what size and quality to write, to `<DIR>/renders/<preset>.mp4` unless
`-o` names another file:

`draft` (the default, also `--draft`): a 540 px proxy on the fastest encoder, without
motion blur unless the theme's `motionBlur` says `always`.

`final` (also `--final`): the video's size at crf 18, blurred unless `motionBlur` is
`off`.

`small`: 720 px at crf 23, a smaller file to share.

Presets are H.264, yuv420p, BT.709, and write the captions as a `.vtt` beside the mp4
when the video is narrated. With video.json's `"captions": true` the captions are also
burned into the frames. Before anything renders, ffmpeg is asked what it was built with:
a missing encoder or demuxer is an error naming it.

Render never narrates: run `oculus studio narrate` first, or it stops with the stale
narration's scene. A frame that fails stops the render, naming its time and scene; an
ffmpeg failure quotes ffmpeg.

oculus studio render lectures/week-4

oculus studio render lectures/week-4 --final -o ~/Desktop/week-4.mp4

oculus studio render lectures/week-4 --preset small

Usage: oculus studio render [OPTIONS] <DIR>

Arguments:
  <DIR>
          The video folder, the one holding `video.json` (or its slug)

Options:
      --draft
          The `draft` preset (the default)

      --final
          The `final` preset

      --preset <NAME>
          The export preset: draft, final or small

  -o, --out <OUT>
          Where to write the file (default: `<DIR>/renders/<preset>.mp4`)

      --threads <T>
          Frame-rendering threads (default: half the cores, capped to keep their memory
          under 2 GB). The encoder runs its own: libx264 always uses 8, so its output is
          the same at any `--threads`

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus studio narrate`

```
Synthesise and time a video's narration, writing narration/manifest.json

Each scene with a `## <id>` section in `script.md` gets a clip: its section text is
spoken by Kokoro inside the app (`--engine kokoro`; read to phonemes through the
lexicon, the dictionary and the guesser) or sent to a TTS server (`--engine server`,
`POST <server>/v1/audio/speech`, WAV), the clip is saved as `narration/<key>.wav`, and
its words are timed against the script with the aligner model (`oculus studio aligner
download` fetches it once). The manifest then gives each narrated scene its length and
its `word()` cues; `frame`, `strip` and `lint` read it. A section is said and timed
whole, then each `[pause]` is spliced in as exact silence between the words either side
of it.

A clip's key hashes its text with its pauses, the engine, the voice and speed, the
server and model or Kokoro's model and the text's phonemes, and the aligner model, so a
run only makes scenes whose text, voice or reading changed (a lexicon edit re-narrates
the scenes it changes); the rest print `cached`. Scenes run one at a time in video order
and the manifest is saved after each, so a failure keeps the scenes before it; the
command then exits 1 naming the failed scene. At the end, entries for scenes no longer
narrated and clips nothing names are deleted.

Per scene it prints the id, `narrated` or `cached`, the clip's length, its word count
and pauses, and as warnings the words the aligner was unsure of and any speech the
script lacks (a mangled or added word: reword it, or listen). `lint` notes the unsure
words and fails on the added speech. With Kokoro, every word the guesser read is then a
`note: check pronunciation` with its scene and script.md line, and the state of any
suggestion for it: listen to it, and suggest a reading for a doubtful one with `oculus
studio pronounce suggest`. Notes never change the exit code.

oculus studio narrate lectures/week-4

oculus studio narrate lectures/week-4 --scene steps --force --voice bf_emma

Usage: oculus studio narrate [OPTIONS] <DIR>

Arguments:
  <DIR>
          The video folder, the one holding `video.json` (or its slug) and `script.md`

Options:
      --scene <ID>
          Only this scene id

      --force
          Make the clips again even when the cached ones match

      --engine <ENGINE>
          `kokoro` runs Kokoro inside the app (`oculus studio voices download` fetches
          it); `server` asks an OpenAI-compatible TTS server

          Possible values:
          - kokoro: Kokoro, run inside the app
          - server: An OpenAI-compatible TTS server

      --server <URL>
          An OpenAI-compatible TTS server, with or without a trailing `/v1` (e.g.
          http://127.0.0.1:8880). Keyless servers only

      --model <MODEL>
          The server's model id (e.g. `kokoro`, or `mlx-community/Kokoro-82M-bf16` on
          mlx-audio)

      --voice <VOICE>
          The voice (e.g. `af_heart`; Kokoro's are listed by `oculus studio voices`)

      --speed <S>
          Speaking rate; 1.0 is the voice's own pace, 1.25 is a quarter faster (unset
          anywhere: 0.9)

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus studio g2p`

```
Show how Kokoro reads text: each word's phonemes and who read it

Reads `TEXT` as `narrate --engine kokoro` would, without synthesising: each word with
its phonemes and its source, `lexicon` (an entry in a lexicon.json), `dict` (misaki's US
dictionary and its rules), `rule` (a heteronym's reading picked by its neighbours) or
`guess` (the guesser, worth a listen), then the phoneme string Kokoro is given. The
lexicon is the global library's (`<app data>/studio/library/lexicon.json`) with the
subject's over it (`<app data>/studio/subjects/<CODE>/lexicon.json`): the subject is
`--subject`, else the video's (`--video`, or the current folder when it holds a
`video.json`). Needs the `g2p-en-us` pack (`oculus studio voices download`). A lexicon
entry that is not valid fails, naming its file and key.

oculus studio g2p "Nesterov and RMSProp adapt the step size."

oculus studio g2p "Cauchy" --subject MAST20004

Usage: oculus studio g2p [OPTIONS] <TEXT>

Arguments:
  <TEXT>
          The text, written as it is said

Options:
      --video <DIR>
          A video folder (or slug) whose subject's lexicon to read

      --subject <CODE>
          The subject whose lexicon to read, over the video's

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus studio pronounce`

```
Suggest how Kokoro should say a word, for the student to review

The lexicon (`lexicon.json`) is written only by the app: an agent that doubts a guessed
word suggests a reading with `suggest`, and the student hears the word's sentence both
ways in Settings -> Studio -> Pronunciation and accepts the suggestion, keeps the guess,
or marks it wrong with a note. An accepted reading or a kept guess goes into the
subject's lexicon (the global library's for a video with no subject) and applies at the
next `narrate`. `list` shows what is still waiting and what was marked wrong.

Usage: oculus studio pronounce <COMMAND>

Commands:
  suggest  Put a reading of a word up for the student's review
  list     List the suggestions waiting for the student, and the ones marked wrong
  help     Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s)

Options:
  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

#### `oculus studio pronounce suggest`

```
Put a reading of a word up for the student's review

Checks `READING` as a lexicon value: a respelling in dictionary words joined by `-` or
spaces, an all-caps part taking the main stress (`NESS-ter-off`), or raw phonemes in
Kokoro's alphabet in slashes (`/nˈɛstəɹˌɔf/`). A part the dictionary lacks or a symbol
Kokoro lacks fails, naming it. Then reads the video's narration with Kokoro's G2P to
find `WORD` (any case; `Word's` counts): its first guessed place, else its first place,
recording how Kokoro reads it now, its sentence, scene and script.md line. A word the
narration never says fails. The suggestion is stored as pending under the video's
subject, replacing an earlier one for the same word; it prints the reading's phonemes.
The student reviews it in Settings -> Studio -> Pronunciation. Needs the `g2p-en-us`
pack.

oculus studio pronounce suggest momentum Nesterov NESS-ter-off

Usage: oculus studio pronounce suggest <DIR> <WORD> <READING>

Arguments:
  <DIR>
          The video folder (or its slug) whose narration says the word

  <WORD>
          The word, as the script spells it

  <READING>
          How to say it: `RE-spell-ing` or `/phonemes/`

Options:
  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

#### `oculus studio pronounce list`

```
List the suggestions waiting for the student, and the ones marked wrong

Newest first: the status (`pending`, or `wrong` with the student's note on how the word
is said), the word, the suggested reading, the subject, video, scene and line. A wrong
one wants another suggestion that follows the note. Decided suggestions are gone: their
reading is in the lexicon.

oculus studio pronounce list --video momentum

Usage: oculus studio pronounce list [OPTIONS]

Options:
      --video <DIR>
          Only this video's (a folder or slug)

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus studio voices`

```
List Kokoro's voices, or download or delete them and its packs

The Kokoro engine narrates inside the app from two packs and a voice, all kept in `<app
data>/models/voice/`, downloaded on request, checked against a pinned size and sha256
and never bundled: `voice-kokoro` (the int8 model, 92 MB), `g2p-en-us` (misaki's US
dictionary and the guesser that reads the words it lacks, 9 MB) and one of the 20 US
English voices (0.5 MB each, graded A to F by Kokoro's authors). With no action it lists
each pack's status and each voice, marking the one Settings -> Studio -> Narration
names.

Usage: oculus studio voices [COMMAND]
```

#### `oculus studio voices download`

```
Download Kokoro's packs and starter voices, or the voices named

With no ID and no `--all`, downloads what a fresh install needs to narrate: the model,
the pronunciation pack and the starter voices `af_heart` and `am_michael`. With IDs, or
with `--all` (all 20), downloads only those voices. Prints progress as it goes; files
already there are kept.

oculus studio voices download

oculus studio voices download am_puck af_bella

oculus studio voices download --all

Usage: oculus studio voices download [OPTIONS] [ID]...

Arguments:
  [ID]...
          Voice ids, as `oculus studio voices` lists them

Options:
      --all
          Every voice

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

#### `oculus studio voices delete`

```
Delete Kokoro's packs, or the voices named

With no ID, deletes the model and the pronunciation pack and any partial download of
them; the voices stay. With IDs, or with `--all`, deletes only those voices.

oculus studio voices delete

oculus studio voices delete am_puck

Usage: oculus studio voices delete [OPTIONS] [ID]...

Arguments:
  [ID]...
          Voice ids, as `oculus studio voices` lists them

Options:
      --all
          Every voice

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus studio agents`

```
Which models a chat agent's Studio subagents run on, and how to start one

For each agent, or only `--agent`'s: the `studio-research` and `studio-scene` roles, the
model and effort Settings -> Jobs gives that agent (its first entry in "Studio research"
and "Studio scenes"), and the exact call that agent makes to start one. A role with no
entry for the agent is off: the agent does that work itself. agy's subagents take no
model, so agy always does it itself. Reads only the settings.

oculus studio agents --agent codex

Usage: oculus studio agents [OPTIONS]

Options:
      --agent <AGENT>
          Only this agent: claude, codex, opencode or antigravity

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

### `oculus studio aligner`

```
Download, check or delete the narration aligner model (378 MB)

`narrate` times each clip's words by forced alignment with a wav2vec2 model run on the
CPU. It is downloaded once, on request, to `<app data>/models/align/`, checked against a
pinned size and sha256, and never bundled with the app.

Usage: oculus studio aligner <COMMAND>

Commands:
  status    Whether the aligner model is downloaded, where, and its size
  download  Download the aligner model, printing progress; does nothing when it is
            already there
  delete    Delete the aligner model and any partial download
  help      Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s)

Options:
  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

## `oculus docs`

```
Write the agent-facing docs into the library

Fills `agents/` in the data directory: `OCULUS-CLI.md`, rendered from this binary's own
`--help` so it can never drift from the flags it documents, one `AGENTS.md` symlinked
into every course folder, and the skills.

It also brings the two generated-but-shared files up to date. `TASTE.md`'s guidance is
re-rendered with the preferences you wrote in it carried across — a file that is half
prompt and half content cannot be "written once and never again" without the prompt half
going stale. Every `MEMORY.md` index is rewritten from the memories beside it.
`OCULUS.md` is the one stub nothing here ever touches twice.

Idempotent, and run by the dev preflight and by `cli:install`, so a library's
instructions always match the binary that is installed.

Usage: oculus docs [OPTIONS]

Options:
      --stdout
          Print the markdown instead of writing the file

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```

## `oculus agent`

```
Run one prompt through a CLI agent and print what it does.

The same bridges the app's chat uses, without the window: the agent runs from the
library's agents/ folder with the app's instructions appended, can read the whole
library and write only there, and its normalized events are printed as they arrive.
Needs the provider's CLI installed and signed in (`claude`, `codex`, `opencode` or
`agy`). Nothing is recorded in the database; this is for checking a bridge works.

Usage: oculus agent [OPTIONS] <PROMPT>

Arguments:
  <PROMPT>
          What to ask

Options:
  -p, --provider <PROVIDER>
          Which CLI to drive

          [default: claude]
          [possible values: claude, codex, opencode, antigravity]

  -m, --model <MODEL>
          Model to request (provider-specific name or alias)

      --effort <EFFORT>
          Codex reasoning effort (low, medium, high, xhigh)

  -s, --subject <SUBJECT_CODE>
          Scope the turn to one subject, as the app's chat does

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')
```
